365.title: The chosen family
365.hook: Allah chose Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran (3:33)
365.howItsDone: Muslims honor the prophets named in 3:33 and their families, and the story of the family of Imran, Maryam's family, is told at length in the surah that bears its name.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zaygh, the swerve, and the prayer after You guided us. Your line was keep my heart straight.

Some families keep a list: a page in the front of an old book, a chart an aunt made, a grandparent who can recite the names back five generations and gets annoyed when you lose track. Al 'Imran is named after a family, and in verse thirty-three it gives its own short list. Four names. Not a family tree in the usual sense: a list of who was chosen, and the doorway to the stories this surah is about to tell.
screen: `A PAGE IN THE FRONT OF AN OLD BOOK.` → `FOUR NAMES.` → `THE DOORWAY TO THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: Pickthall translates 3:33: "Lo! Allah preferred Adam and Noah and the Family of Abraham and the Family of 'Imran above (all His) creatures." Adam, where the human story begins, as the Qur'an tells it. Nuh, Noah, who carried the survivors through the flood. The family of Ibrahim, running through Isma'il and Ishaq to a long line of prophets, and, Muslims believe, to Muhammad ﷺ. And the family of Imran. Who is Imran? The Qur'an calls Maryam, the mother of Isa, the daughter of Imran, and many commentators take this to be her father. Others connected the name to Amram, the father of Musa and Harun. The verse doesn't say, and both views appear in the classical books. The verb is istafa, from a root meaning purity, the clear, best part of something. The Prophet's title al-Mustafa, the chosen one, comes from the same root. Then 3:34, in Pickthall's words: "They were descendants one of another." One line, linked from Adam onward. But chosen doesn't mean easy, and the surah shows it right away: Imran's wife, pregnant, promises her unborn child to God, and is surprised when the child is a girl. That girl is Maryam. Over the next days come Zakariyya, who looked after her, and the angels who spoke to her. Being chosen, in these stories, isn't a badge. It's a weight passed hand to hand, and each person in the line had to carry it in their own hard moment.

segments.voice: Think back along your own line: a parent, a grandparent, someone further back whose name you only half know, or, if family is complicated, whoever raised you, taught you or held you up, because a line doesn't have to be only blood. Pick one person and name one thing they passed to you, a habit, a phrase, a way of standing. If you pray, you can thank God for them, in whatever words are yours.
Istafa, chose, the purest part of something. Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran, chosen, and descendants one of another. Today's word.
Your line: a chosen line. What was handed to you is part of yours. Until tomorrow.

366.title: Zakariyya's silence
366.hook: his sign is three days without speaking except by gesture, and remembering Allah (3:41)
366.tomorrow: Maryam above the women of the worlds
366.howItsDone: Muslims honor Zakariyya and Yahya as prophets; his story (3:37–41 and Surah Maryam) is often recited by those hoping for a child, and his sign of silence filled with remembrance is a model for quiet dhikr in the morning and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday: istafa, the chosen family, Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran. Your line was a chosen line.

An old man walks into a small prayer room to check on the girl he's raising. She's Maryam; he's her guardian, Zakariyya. Beside her is food he didn't bring. Where did this come from, he asks. From God, she says; God provides for whom He wills, beyond counting. And the old man, who has no children and a wife who never could, stands right there and starts to pray for a child of his own.
screen: `A SMALL PRAYER ROOM.` → `FOOD HE DIDN'T BRING.` → `AN OLD MAN STARTS TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: That's 3:37 and 38. The prayer room is the mihrab, the same word used today for the niche in a mosque's wall that shows the direction of prayer. What Zakariyya saw there made him brave enough to ask. Then 3:39: while he's still standing in prayer, the angels call to him with good news of a son, Yahya, who will confirm a word from God, noble, chaste, and a prophet. And Zakariyya, who has just asked for exactly this, asks how. I'm old. My wife is barren. The answer, in Pickthall's words: "So (it will be). Allah doeth what He will." He asks for a sign, and the sign is strange. In 3:41 he won't speak to people for three days, except by ramz, by gesture. And: remember your Lord much, and glorify Him in the evening and the morning. In Surah Maryam, the nineteenth, the same sign is three nights, and he comes out and signals to his people to glorify God morning and evening. Commentators differ on why it came this way. Some read the silence as a mercy, a sign he could feel in his own body. Others note his tongue was stopped from talk with people, never from remembering God. Christians tell a story of the same man, Zechariah, in the Gospel of Luke. In the Qur'an's telling, the point lands on what filled the silence: no small talk, no explaining, no complaining. Only gestures, and dhikr, remembrance, morning and evening.

segments.voice: Close your mouth gently and let the silence settle, noticing how much talk runs inside you even when you aren't speaking. Each time a sentence starts to form, let it go and come back to one simple remembrance: if you pray, subhanallah, glory be to God, and if you don't, simply the breath.

367.title: Maryam above the women of the worlds
367.hook: the angels say Allah has chosen and purified her (3:42–43)
367.howItsDone: Muslims hold Maryam in deep honor as the mother of the prophet Isa and, following the hadith, among the best of women; Surah Maryam (19) and her verses in Al 'Imran are recited and taught, and girls are often named after her.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Zakariyya's silence, three days of gesture filled with remembrance. Your line was silent and remembering.

Readers of the Qur'an point something out about Maryam: a queen appears in it, and prophets' wives and mothers, but tradition counts her as the one woman the book calls by her own name. A whole surah, the nineteenth, carries it. And here in Al 'Imran, the girl Zakariyya was raising has grown up, and the angels speak to her directly, with words that set her above the women of the worlds.
screen: `CALLED BY HER OWN NAME.` → `A SURAH CARRIES HER NAME.` → `THE ANGELS SPEAK TO HER.`

segments.voice: In 3:42 the angels say: O Maryam, God has chosen you and purified you, and chosen you above the women of the worlds. Listen to the shape of it. Chosen, istafa, the word from two days ago with the family of Imran, comes twice. Commentators explain the two choosings differently: some say the first is being chosen for devotion and accepted in the sanctuary, and the second is being chosen above all women, for the birth of Isa. Between them, purified: kept clean of what would stain her. Then 3:43 gives her the instructions any worshiper gets: be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow. A young woman, alone in a sanctuary, addressed by angels, and told to pray. Verse 44 adds a scene from her childhood: the men of the temple cast their pens, like drawing lots, to decide who would care for her, and argued over the honor. Zakariyya won. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is reported, in Sahih al-Bukhari, to have said that the best of the women of her time was Maryam, and the best of the women of his own time was Khadijah, his wife. A hadith in Tirmidhi names four women who are enough, among all the women of the world, to look to: Maryam, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, Khadijah, and Fatimah his daughter. Christians honor her too, as Mary, and the two traditions tell her story in their own ways. In the Qur'an's telling, her greatness isn't fame. It's two choosings, one purifying, and a life of bowing in prayer.

368.title: A common word
368.hook: come to a word common between us: to worship none but Allah (3:64)
368.howItsDone: Muslims cite 3:64 in interfaith conversation; in 2007 Muslim scholars and leaders addressed an open letter titled 'A Common Word Between Us and You' to Christian leaders, built on love of God and love of neighbor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maryam, chosen above the women of the worlds. Your line was chosen and purified.

October 2007. A letter goes out from Muslim scholars and leaders, more than a hundred and thirty of them, Sunni and Shia, from many countries. It's addressed to the Pope, to Orthodox patriarchs, to the Archbishop of Canterbury, and to the leaders of Christian churches everywhere. Its title is a phrase lifted straight out of a verse in Al 'Imran: a common word between us and you.
screen: `OCTOBER 2007.` → `A LETTER TO CHURCH LEADERS.` → `A PHRASE FROM AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:64 in Pickthall's words: "Say: O People of the Scripture! Come to an agreement between us and you: that we shall worship none but Allah." Pickthall says agreement. The Arabic is kalimatin sawa', a word that is level, the same for both sides. People of the Scripture, ahl al-kitab, is the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians, those given scripture before, in the Qur'an's terms. The verse goes on: that we ascribe no partner to God, and that none of us take others as lords beside God. And if they turn away, say: bear witness that we are Muslims, those who have surrendered. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't threaten. It invites, names the ground it believes both sides share, and if the answer is no, it asks the other side to witness where Muslims stand. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir connect this part of the surah to a delegation of Christians from Najran who came to Medina to talk with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet wrote to Heraclius, the Byzantine emperor, his letter included this very verse. The 2007 letter built on two commandments it found in both scriptures: love of God, and love of neighbor. Christian leaders wrote back, and meetings followed. Muslims and Christians still differ on central things, and the verse itself names some of them. But it opens with the word common.
screen: `KALIMATIN SAWA': A LEVEL WORD` · `AHL AL-KITAB: PEOPLE OF THE SCRIPTURE` · `AN INVITATION, NOT A THREAT` · `FROM HERACLIUS TO 2007` · then, large: `COME TO A COMMON WORD.`

segments.voice: Picture a table between you and a neighbor, coworker or relative whose beliefs aren't yours, and instead of your differences, set down the things you both care about: the people you love, honesty, a good day's work, maybe a God you each pray to in your own way. Look at what's on the table and find one sentence you could both say and mean.

369.title: The rope of Allah
369.hook: hold fast together to the rope of Allah and don't divide (3:103)
369.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 3:103 in sermons and community gatherings as a call to unity, and many read the 'rope of Allah' as the Qur'an, the shared book that holds the community together.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalimatin sawa', a word level between us and you. Your line was start from what is shared.

Before the Prophet ﷺ came to Medina, the city had two great Arab tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj. The reports call them kin, with a long history of feuds and revenge, ending in a battle called Bu'ath not long before. Then both tribes became Muslim, and sat in the same rows to pray, with dead relatives between them. Today's verse was spoken into that room.
screen: `TWO TRIBES OF MEDINA.` → `A LONG FEUD.` → `THE SAME ROWS TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Pickthall translates 3:103: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." Cable, rope: the Arabic is habl, a rope you hold so you don't fall. And all of you together is part of the command. It isn't a rope for one person to cling to alone. The verse goes on: remember God's favor to you, how you were enemies, and He joined your hearts, and by His grace you became brothers. You were on the edge of a pit of fire, and He saved you from it. Commentators hear the Aws and the Khazraj in it, though the verse names no one. The major tafsir works tell of a man who tried to reopen the old wound by having someone recite poems from the war days. Tempers flared, hands went to weapons, and the Prophet came out and reminded them who they now were. What is the rope? Commentators give several answers. Some say the Qur'an itself, and a report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet call the Book of God a rope stretched from heaven to earth. Others say the covenant with God, or the community of believers, or sincere faith. These answers don't fight each other: many hands can hold one rope. And a rope doesn't make everyone stand in the same spot. People hold it at different points, some near, some far. It only asks that you don't let go, and that you don't cut it.
screen: `HABL: A ROPE YOU HOLD` · `ALL OF YOU, TOGETHER` · `ENEMIES MADE BROTHERS` · `WHAT IS THE ROPE?` · then, large: `HOLD FAST, AND DO NOT SEPARATE.`

segments.voice: Picture your own circle, family, friends, a mosque, a team at work, and somewhere in it a split, small or old: two people who don't talk, or you and someone you've drifted from. Picture one rope you're both holding at different points, and ask what one small pull toward each other would look like: a message, a greeting, a kind word about them to someone else.

370.title: Calling to good
370.hook: let there be a people inviting to good and forbidding wrong (3:104)
370.howItsDone: Muslims describe enjoining good and forbidding wrong as a communal duty; in practice it ranges from encouraging prayer and charity to gently advising friends, with scholars stressing knowledge, gentleness and avoiding greater harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday: habl, the rope of Allah, held by everyone together. Your line was hold the rope together.

Every group chat has one. The person who posts the fundraiser link, reminds everyone it's someone's birthday, suggests visiting the friend in the hospital, and now and then says gently, maybe let's not share that. Sometimes people roll their eyes. The group would miss them if they left. The very next verse after the rope of Allah describes a whole community of people like that, and gives them a job description.
screen: `THE ONE IN THE GROUP CHAT.` → `THE BIRTHDAY, THE HOSPITAL VISIT.` → `A JOB DESCRIPTION.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, 3:104 says: "And there may spring from you a nation who invite to goodness, and enjoin right conduct and forbid indecency. Such are they who are successful." Inside it is a famous phrase, al-amr bil-ma'ruf wan-nahy 'an al-munkar: enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Ma'ruf comes from a root meaning to know: the recognized good, the kind decent people know when they see it. Munkar is what's rejected, what people recognize as not right. And the verse starts with invite. The open door comes before any correcting. Scholars noticed a small word too: min, from you. Does it mean a group among you should do this, or that all of you should be this kind of people? Some classical scholars read it as some among you, a duty a part of the community fulfills for everyone. Others read it as describing the whole community. A well-known hadith in Sahih Muslim sets out the steps: whoever sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he can't, then with his tongue; if he can't, then in his heart, and that is the weakest of faith. Scholars such as al-Ghazali attached conditions: know the matter well, act gently, and don't cause a greater harm than the one you're stopping. So the verse isn't a license to police strangers. It begins with the person who invites, and the good it means is the kind everyone recognizes.
screen: `INVITE, ENJOIN, FORBID` · `MA'RUF: THE GOOD EVERYONE KNOWS` · `SOME OF YOU, OR ALL OF YOU?` · `HAND, TONGUE, HEART` · then, large: `A PEOPLE WHO INVITE TO GOODNESS.`

fork.setup: you see something wrong, but you can't change it with your hands. according to the hadith in Sahih Muslim, what's next?
options: do nothing; it's not your business.
change it with your tongue, by speaking.
wait for someone else to act.
fork.reveal: hand, then tongue, then heart. the heart is the last step, and the hadith calls it the weakest of faith.

original.note: Arabic: the known, the recognized good (3:104), from the root '-r-f, to know.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious people telling others what to do.
what it means: a community that first invites to good, encourages the recognized right and resists the recognized wrong.
what a scholar hears: ma'ruf and munkar as the known and the rejected; and the old debate over whether 'min' in 3:104 means some of you or all of you.
recall: a word level between both sides

chat.says: Does 'enjoin good, forbid wrong' mean Muslims should police other people?
options: 3:104 starts with invite; scholars add: know the matter, act gently, cause no greater harm.
Yes: 3:104 tells every Muslim to police strangers as strictly as they can.
No: it's only about your own heart, never about speaking or acting at all.
chat.meaning: 3:104 begins with inviting to goodness. Scholars such as al-Ghazali added conditions: know the matter, act gently, don't cause a greater harm.

ma'ruf.meaning: the known good, what decent people recognize

munkar.meaning: the wrong, what people recognize as not right

al-Ghazali.meaning: a classical scholar who set conditions for correcting wrong

sources.ref: tafsir on 3:104 (the meaning of 'min'), e.g. al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir; conditions of hisba in al-Ghazali's Ihya'

371.title: Don't lose heart
371.hook: after Uhud: don't weaken or grieve, days of fortune rotate among people (3:139–140)
371.howItsDone: Muslims remember Uhud and its martyrs, including Hamzah, the Prophet's uncle, and the verses of Al 'Imran revealed after the battle are often recited for comfort after loss and defeat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'ruf, the good everyone knows, and your line, invite to good.

A year after their first victory at Badr, the Muslims of Medina met a much larger army from Mecca at the foot of a mountain called Uhud. The battle started well. Then a group of archers, told by the Prophet ﷺ never to leave their hill, saw the enemy running and came down for the spoils. The cavalry swept around behind them. Many Muslims died, among them the Prophet's uncle Hamzah, and the Prophet himself was wounded. They walked home to a city in mourning.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN OF UHUD.` → `THE ARCHERS LEAVE THE HILL.` → `A CITY IN MOURNING.`

segments.voice: A large part of Al 'Imran, from around verse 121, speaks into the days after that loss. It doesn't pretend the defeat didn't happen, or hide the mistake. But 3:139 says, in Pickthall's words: "Faint not nor grieve." And 3:140 gives a surprising reason. If a wound has touched you, a wound like it touched the other side too, at Badr. Then: these are the days, and We make them take turns among people. The verb is nudawiluha, from the root d-w-l, to rotate, to pass from hand to hand. The same root gives dawla, which today means a state, a country, but at heart means a turn: power is something that rotates. So the verse doesn't promise you'll always win. It says the days turn, for everyone. Good days and bad days are passed around, and neither one stays forever. The verse adds that this is how God makes known who truly believes, and takes witnesses, shuhada, from among them: the martyrs of Uhud. There's grief in it, and dignity. And this week built toward it: a chosen family carrying a weight, Zakariyya's silence, Maryam, a common word, the rope, a people who call to good. Now a community knocked down, and told: don't lose heart. The days turn.
screen: `NOT HIDING THE LOSS` · `FAINT NOT NOR GRIEVE` · `D-W-L: THE DAYS TAKE TURNS` · `A WEEK BUILDING TO THIS` · then, large: `THESE ARE THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a recent loss or setback, small or large, and feel it honestly; the verse doesn't ask anyone to pretend. Then remember a day in your past that felt just as bad and has since turned, a day you got through, and breathe with both of them. If you pray, you can ask God for steadiness.
Nudawiluha, we make them take turns. Spoken to the Muslims after Uhud: faint not nor grieve, the days take turns among people. Today's word.
Your line: days turn. Uhud's grief was real, and so was the turning. A week, done.

guess: We make them take turns, hand to hand
We record them in the book of deeds
We count them until the Last Day

pairs: left their hill for the spoils

myth: the Qur'an hides the defeat at Uhud
a long passage of Al 'Imran speaks openly about the loss and the mistake.
the Arabic for 'take turns' shares a root with dawla
d-w-l: to rotate; dawla, a state, at heart means a turn.
the verse promises believers will always win
it says the days take turns among people.

fork.setup: you're one of the archers at Uhud. the Prophet told you never to leave the hill. you see the enemy running. what happened?
options: all the archers stayed at their post.
many came down for the spoils, and the cavalry swept around behind.
the archers chased the enemy back to Mecca.
fork.reveal: many left the hill, the enemy cavalry came round behind, and a winning battle turned into a painful loss.

original.note: Arabic: We make them take turns (3:140), said of the days; root d-w-l, to rotate.

trapdoor: what you thought: God's people never lose.
what it means: after a real defeat, the verse says don't weaken or grieve; the days take turns among people.
what a scholar hears: nudawiluha, from d-w-l, the root of dawla, a turn of power; and shuhada in 3:140, witnesses, read as the martyrs of Uhud.

chat.says: After a defeat like Uhud, what did the Qur'an tell the Muslims?
options: Faint not nor grieve: the other side was wounded too, and the days take turns.
That they'd lost because God had abandoned them for good after Badr.
That the defeat never really happened, so they should just forget it.
chat.meaning: 3:139–140: faint not nor grieve. A wound touched the other side too, and God makes these days take turns among people.

Uhud.meaning: the mountain near Medina where the battle was fought

Badr.meaning: the Muslims' first victory, a year before Uhud

Hamzah.meaning: the Prophet's uncle, killed at Uhud

dawla.meaning: a state, a country; at heart, a turn

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the Battle of Uhud)
